implementation_notes: Kotlin's coroutine library is the idiomatic home: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex.tryLock() 'tries to lock this mutex, returning false if it is already locked' instead of suspending, and Channel.trySend() never suspends and reports the outcome through a ChannelResult - both are exact balking primitives and fit structured concurrency, where blocking a thread is not allowed. On the JVM side java.util.concurrent remains available (ReentrantLock.tryLock, Semaphore.tryAcquire) for thread-based code, and a plain synchronized block is the fallback for shared state. Use the suspending variants (withLock, send) whenever the caller must eventually proceed rather than balk.
pitfalls: Mutex.tryLock() returns false when the mutex is already locked; it throws IllegalStateException only when a non-null owner token matches the current owner, so do not pass the same owner token to a re-entrant attempt.
Channel.trySend() drops the element when the buffer is full or the channel is closed: inspect the returned ChannelResult (isFailure/isClosed) instead of assuming delivery.
Every successful tryLock must reach the finally-unlock on the balking path too, or the state machine wedges for all coroutines.
